flagged.problem: For private hosted zones and Resolver rules, the answer (False) is right. But the statement says "a VPC's local DNS settings" in general, and a Profile also carries DNS Firewall rule groups. Those are ordered by priority, not by local-wins precedence. The card should name the resource type the documented rule covers.
flagged.suggestedFix: Replacement (answer False). Statement: "When a VPC's own private hosted zone and its Route 53 Profile's zone share a domain name, the Profile's zone answers." Explanation: "When a query matches a private hosted zone associated directly with the VPC and one associated through its Route 53 Profile, the VPC's local setting wins; otherwise the most specific domain name wins." Keep the URL profiles.html and keep volatility may_change.

verdicts.notes:
I checked all 10 section 1.3 cards (5 True, 5 False; average statement length 98.8 for both answers). I downloaded every source URL with curl (all returned 200, all on docs.aws.amazon.com and current) and matched the text myself, without relying on summaries. Nine cards pass; only 1.3-04 is flagged.

Quotes that settle the passing cards:
- 01, True. DR whitepaper: "pilot light cannot process requests without additional action taken first, whereas warm standby can handle traffic (at reduced capacity levels) immediately."
- 02, False. DR whitepaper: "data corruption may need to rely on backups, which usually results in a non-zero recovery point". Also: "Continuous data replication ... may not protect you against data corruption or destruction unless your strategy also includes versioning of stored data or options for point-in-time recovery."
- 03, True. DR whitepaper: "For maximum resiliency, you should use only data plane operations as part of your failover operation. This is because the data planes typically have higher availability design goals than the control planes."
- 05, True. what-is-drs: "launch recovery instances on AWS within minutes, using the most up-to-date server state or a previous point in time."
- 06, True. create-cross-account-backup: "AWS Backup re-encrypts your copy using the encryption key of your destination vault."
- 07, False. point-in-time-recovery: "You can't create copies of Amazon RDS continuous backups because AWS Backup for Amazon RDS does not allow copying transaction logs. Instead, AWS Backup creates a snapshot and copies it".
- 08, True. logicallyairgappedvault: "Is automatically set with a vault lock in compliance mode".
- 09, False. logicallyairgappedvault: "The vault cannot be shared with an entire organization or with organizational units (OUs) — only individual account IDs are supported as share principals."
- 10, False. cross-region-backup: "AWS Backup does not support cross-Region copies for storage in cold tiers." The copy page goes further: "backups in cold storage or archive tiers cannot be copied", which covers cross-account copies too.

Minor points below the flag threshold:
- 06: encryption.html documents an exception: "Copies of unencrypted Amazon Aurora, Amazon DocumentDB, and Amazon Neptune clusters are also unencrypted." The cited page states the rule without that caveat, so the card holds. An optional tightening would be "re-encrypts an encrypted cross-account backup copy".
- 07: Amazon RDS has its own cross-Region automated backup replication, which does keep PITR. The statement names AWS Backup, so the answer stands, but naming the RDS feature in the explanation would make the card more useful.
- 09: the explanation's first sentence is ungrammatical ("AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault shares name individual account IDs"). A suggested rewrite: "AWS Backup shares a logically air-gapped vault only with individual account IDs, in the same or another organization."
- Breadth: six of the ten cards are about AWS Backup and three are DR strategy cards. The scope items scale-up versus scale-out and automatic recovery from failure have no card. That is worth fixing in a later round, but no single card is wrong because of it.

Duplicate check: no other section rests on the same facts. The closest card is 3.4-03 (DynamoDB point-in-time restore into a new table), which tests a different fact from 02 and 07.

cards.statement: For the same domain, a Route 53 Profile's private hosted zone overrides one associated directly with the VPC.
cards.explanation: When a query matches a private hosted zone associated directly with the VPC and one associated through its Route 53 Profile, the VPC's local setting wins; otherwise the most specific domain name wins.
cards.reason: Wording lens fix applied: 'the VPC's own zone' could be read as an Availability Zone. Fact confirmed on profiles.html today: the local DNS settings take precedence and the example.com/example.com row evaluates to Local VPC. 109 chars.

cards.statement: A GuardDuty delegated administrator designated in one Region manages member accounts only in that Region.
cards.explanation: GuardDuty administration is Regional: the delegated administrator and its members are added in each Region where GuardDuty is enabled, and the same account must be the administrator in every Region.
cards.reason: Both lenses flagged 'manages ... alone' as ambiguous and proposed 'only'; merged into the shorter fact-lens text (105 chars). guardduty_organizations.html confirmed today: 'will only manage member accounts added to the organization in that Region' (so the absolute is sourced), plus 'use the same account ... in all other Regions'.

cards.statement: AWS RAM can share an AWS Backup logically air-gapped vault with an organizational unit.
cards.explanation: AWS Backup shares a logically air-gapped vault through AWS RAM with individual account IDs, in the same or another organization; OUs and whole organizations are not accepted as share principals.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The fact lens quoted logicallyairgappedvault.html directly, and the prompt's continuity trap says the same.

cards.statement: A Savings Plan keeps discounting its former organization's consolidated bill after its owner account leaves.
cards.explanation: If a Savings Plan's owner account leaves an organization, the plan no longer applies to that organization's consolidated bill, so the remaining accounts lose its discount.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. ri-turn-off.html says this directly, and the prompt's cost trap says the same.

cards.statement: A StackSet with service-managed permissions skips the management account, even when that account sits in a target OU.
cards.explanation: CloudFormation doesn't deploy service-managed StackSet instances to the management account, even when it belongs to a targeted OU, so that account needs its own stack for the same baseline.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The fact lens quoted the Considerations sentence from the StackSets page.

cards.statement: By default, a State Manager association reruns on a managed node that comes back online after missing a scheduled run.
cards.explanation: Besides its schedule, State Manager runs an association when a node first comes online or returns after a missed run, unless the association is set to apply only at its next cron interval.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The narrow Automation-runbook exception the fact lens noted does not change the general rule.

cards.statement: ARC Region switch can include application resources from separate AWS accounts in one recovery plan.
cards.explanation: Region switch supports application resources in multiple accounts and can share plans across accounts, so one team can orchestrate a Regional recovery for a multi-account application.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it, and region-switch.html supports cross-account resources. Keep volatility may_change.

cards.statement: A security group rule can reference a security group in a peered VPC that is in another Region.
cards.explanation: Security group references across a VPC peering connection work only when both VPCs are in the same Region, in the same or another account. For an inter-Region peer, rules use the peer VPC's CIDR block.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. vpc-peering-security-groups.html supports every clause.

cards.statement: ARC zonal autoshift can move an application's traffic out of an Availability Zone where its resources are healthy.
cards.explanation: AWS starts an autoshift from its own telemetry of an Availability Zone impairment and does not inspect individual resource health, so AWS recommends pre-scaling capacity in the other zones.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The page says ARC does not inspect individual resource health and recommends pre-scaling.

cards.statement: When a Multi-AZ Redis OSS primary fails, Amazon ElastiCache promotes the replica with the least replication lag.
cards.explanation: ElastiCache promotes the most current replica, which minimizes data lost to asynchronous replication. Writes resume within seconds through the unchanged primary endpoint.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. AutoFailover.html quotes match, and the Valkey 9.0 durability exception does not apply to Redis OSS.

cards.statement: Amazon Route 53 IP-based routing can steer hybrid clients by address range for records in a private hosted zone.
cards.explanation: Route 53 IP-based routing applies to public hosted zones. An architect chooses a different routing approach for records in a private hosted zone.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The page says IP-based routing can't be used for records in a private hosted zone, and the tell is removed.

cards.statement: An ElastiCache for Redis OSS cluster with multiple shards spreads write-heavy traffic across several primaries.
cards.explanation: Cluster mode enabled distributes Redis OSS data across shards, with a primary accepting writes for its shard. Additional write endpoints help a design scale a write-heavy cache.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The wording lens's minor guessability note is not a reason to drop the card.

cards.statement: Amazon RDS for MySQL adds read replicas to a DB instance automatically when the instance's read traffic grows.
cards.explanation: RDS doesn't autoscale read replicas: an architect creates and deletes them, so a design with spiky read demand needs its own scaling logic.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. USER_ReadRepl.html says twice that RDS doesn't support read replica autoscaling.

cards.statement: Amazon MemoryDB can replace a cache plus a separate durable database as a microservice's primary data store.
cards.explanation: MemoryDB serves data from memory and stores it durably across Availability Zones in a Multi-AZ transactional log, so one service can act as a high-performance primary database.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. what-is-memorydb.html says this almost word for word.

cards.statement: DynamoDB adaptive capacity can isolate a single heavily accessed item on its own partition to reduce throttling.
cards.explanation: Adaptive capacity rebalances partitions so frequently accessed items stop sharing one. An isolated item still gets at most one partition's maximum throughput.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. 'can' matches the page's 'might', and the partition maximum is on the page.

cards.statement: S3 Intelligent-Tiering charges a retrieval fee when an application reads an object from its Infrequent Access tier.
cards.explanation: S3 Intelligent-Tiering has no retrieval fees; it charges a small monthly monitoring and automation fee per object, which suits data with unknown or changing access patterns.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. storage-class-intro.html says there are no retrieval fees for Intelligent-Tiering.

cards.statement: By default, Amazon Inspector stops rescanning an ECR image not pushed or used within the configured re-scan durations.
cards.explanation: Inspector rescans an ECR image while its push date or, in the default mode, its last-in-use date is within the configured durations; after that it marks the image inactive and closes its findings.
cards.reason: Fact lens fix applied: the page offers a Last pull date mode in which a recently pulled image keeps being rescanned, so the claim holds only in the default Last in use date mode. The lens's statement was 129 chars, so I shortened it to 118 using the page's own wording ('hasn't been pushed or last used ... within the configured push and last in use dates'). Confirmed on the page today: Last in use date is the default mode, and expired images are set to inactive with their findings scheduled to close. Explanation is 196 chars.

cards.statement: Launching several instance types into one EC2 cluster placement group improves the odds that the launch finds capacity.
cards.explanation: AWS allows mixed instance types in a cluster placement group but says this reduces the chance that the required capacity is available; it recommends one instance type launched in a single request.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. placement-strategies.html states both the lower chance of capacity and the recommendation.

cards.statement: With instance weights, an Auto Scaling group keeps its current capacity at or below the desired capacity in units.
cards.explanation: Current capacity can exceed desired capacity when a launched instance carries more units than remain to be filled, so AWS advises a desired capacity two to three times the largest weight.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The page states the overshoot and the two-to-three-times advice, and the causal 'so' is a reasonable inference.

cards.statement: When Elastic Load Balancing reports every instance unhealthy, Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling can throttle their replacement.
cards.explanation: If ELB health checks report all instances unhealthy while the load balancer is InService, Auto Scaling might mark fewer of them unhealthy at a time, leaving time to fix the fault before the whole group is replaced.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. health-checks-overview.html uses the 'throttle' wording. Explanation is 214 chars.

cards.statement: Updating a Service Quotas request template requests its new quota values for existing accounts in the organization.
cards.explanation: A quota request template requests its values for accounts created in the organization after association. Updating it leaves existing accounts' quotas unchanged, so they need their own increase requests.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. organization-templates.html states this directly.

cards.statement: An instance reuse policy makes Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling return scaled-in instances to the group's warm pool.
cards.explanation: An instance reuse policy sends scaled-in instances back to the warm pool. A workload with lengthy initialization reuses prepared instances when demand grows again.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The warm pools page confirms that instances are terminated by default and that a reuse policy returns them to the pool.

cards.statement: A CloudWatch billing alarm compares projected month-end charges with its threshold to prompt cost intervention.
cards.explanation: CloudWatch billing alarms compare current estimated charges with the threshold. Their billing metric reflects accrued costs rather than a projection of the month's final bill.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The page says the alarm doesn't use projections.

cards.statement: Deleting an older incremental Amazon EBS snapshot removes block data that the volume's newer snapshots still reference.
cards.explanation: EBS removes only data referenced exclusively by the deleted snapshot and keeps blocks that later snapshots use, so deleting old snapshots might not reduce storage costs.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. ebs-deleting-snapshot.html supports every clause, and the SOA deck card is close but not a duplicate within this deck.

cards.statement: AWS wave planning guidance filters shared services such as Active Directory out of dependency data before grouping.
cards.explanation: Shared services such as Active Directory, backup and monitoring connect to almost everything and would glue the portfolio into one group, so the guidance excludes them when deriving dependency groups.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The wave-planning page says to filter out shared services such as Active Directory.

cards.statement: AWS DMS bidirectional replication resolves conflicting updates made to the same rows on both databases.
cards.explanation: DMS bidirectional replication runs two tasks with loopback prevention but has no conflict detection or resolution, so a fallback design keeps each data element written on one side only.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. CHAP_Task.CDC.html says bidirectional replication doesn't include conflict detection or resolution.

cards.statement: AD Connector caches directory data in AWS so Amazon WorkSpaces users can sign in while the on-premises link is down.
cards.explanation: AD Connector is a directory gateway that redirects requests to on-premises Active Directory without caching any information in the cloud, so sign-ins depend on connectivity to that directory.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The page's opening sentence says AD Connector works 'without caching any information in the cloud'.

cards.statement: Volume Gateway stored volumes keep the primary data in Amazon S3 and hold a local copy of frequently accessed subsets.
cards.explanation: Stored volumes keep the full dataset on premises and asynchronously back up point-in-time snapshots to Amazon S3; cached volumes are the option that keeps primary data in S3.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. WhatIsStorageGateway.html defines cached and stored volumes exactly this way.

cards.statement: Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ supports XA distributed transactions for JMS applications leaving a commercial broker.
cards.explanation: Amazon MQ supports standard JMS features, including JMS and distributed (XA) transactions, so an application leaving IBM MQ or TIBCO EMS can keep its transaction semantics with minimal code changes.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. The migration guide lists XA transactions and the commercial-broker migration context.

cards.statement: An Amazon EventBridge replay can name an event bus other than its archive's source bus as the replay destination.
cards.explanation: Archived events can be replayed only to the archive's source event bus. A replay can be limited to chosen rules on that bus, whose targets then receive the events.
cards.reason: Both lenses keep it. eb-archive.html says archived events can only be replayed to the source event bus.
